title: The Polymarketification of American Life
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
The Polymarketification of American Life

Prediction markets have been trying to skirt regulators by selling themselves not as sportsbooks but as insurance.

On January 8, 2025, as the Palisades fire consumed the neighborhoods perched on the hills above Los Angeles, a website called Polymarket rushed to open a series of betting markets on the disaster. Users could wager on anything from how many acres would burn by Friday to when the blaze would reach Santa Monica. Some of the pools climbed past $100,000. Polymarket posted updates to its social media account as the odds shifted, with the cheerful specificity of a weather service: There was a 91 percent chance, the platform announced on X, that the Palisades fire would exceed ten thousand acres by Friday. “That’s 12x the size of Central Park,” the post helpfully added.

The backlash was instant. On social media, users called the markets “sick” and “disgusting.” Some raised the obvious and uncomfortable point that a market paying out when the fire spread created a financial incentive to feed it. By the time more than one hundred thousand people were under evacuation orders, Polymarket had become a national story, and not in the way a company usually wants to become one.

The platform was ready for the backlash, posting a disclaimer directly on the wildfire market page. The goal of Polymarket, it explained, was to create “accurate, unbiased forecasts” for important events. “The devastating Pacific Palisades fire is one such event, for which Polymarket can yield invaluable real-time answers to those directly impacted in ways traditional media cannot.” According to Polymarket, it was providing a public service.

It was a remarkable argument, and one that many observers were shocked by. The people losing their homes didn’t seem particularly in need of real-time betting odds on whether those homes would burn. But Polymarket’s defense was aimed not at evacuees but at regulators and legislators, meant to address the question that has followed the company and its competitors since the moment they started operating: Is this gambling, or is it investing? Is it entertainment or a financial instrument? The prediction market industry had something else entirely in mind. The concept it reached for, in regulatory filings and funding announcements and interviews, was not “forecasting tool” but something more familiar and respectable: “insurance.”

At the same moment that Polymarket’s wildfire markets were drawing national outrage, Pacific Palisades residents were dealing with a more consequential controversy than six-figure wagers on whether their homes would burn. State Farm, California’s largest home insurer, had recently canceled thirty thousand home insurance policies across the state. Sixteen hundred of those canceled policies were in Pacific Palisades. These homes had been deemed too much of a liability by an industry that spent a century and a half insisting it was in the business of protecting people from exactly these types of disasters. Now these homeowners watched their homes burn while a cryptocurrency platform wagered on the outcome and called it a public service. The insurance industry had abandoned them. A prediction market had shown up in its place, wearing its clothes.

Prediction markets—exchanges where users can bet on not just sports but politics, the weather, even words Trump might say in his next public address—occupy a strange position in American life right now. They are simultaneously the most exciting thing in finance and the most wanted fugitive by state gambling regulators and legislators. Platforms like Polymarket have exploded in the past two years, attracting billions of dollars in investment, partnerships with the New York Stock Exchange and CNBC, and enough trading volume to make their odds a fixture of cable news chyrons.
